problem: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) accuracy becomes increasingly challenging as document corpora scale up, with retrievers playing an outsized role by extracting relevant documents to provide context to LLMs (p.1). Finding the best search method for RAG is an emerging area of research, and current retrieval methodologies relying on keyword and similarity searches restrict overall accuracy (p.1).
methodology: The study proposes 'Blended RAG' by leveraging semantic search techniques such as Dense Vector indexes and Sparse Encoder indexes blended with hybrid query strategies across multiple fields like Cross Fields, Most Fields, Best Fields, and Phrase Prefix (p.1, p.2). The best-performing hybrid queries and indices (sextet retrievers) are integrated into a generative question-answering RAG pipeline using the FLAN-T5-XXL model under zero-shot learning (p.2, p.5).
dataset: The study evaluates retrievers and RAG pipelines on several datasets including Natural Questions (NQ), TREC-COVID, Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD), HotPotQA, and CoQA (p.2, p.4, p.5, p.6).
results: On the NQ dataset, the hybrid query with Sparse Encoder and Best Fields achieved an 88.77% top-10 retrieval accuracy, and the pipeline provided an NDCG@10 score of 0.67 (p.2, p.4). On the TREC-COVID dataset, the Sparse Encoder with Best Fields achieved a 98% top-10 retrieval accuracy for score-2 and an NDCG@10 score of 0.87 (p.3, p.4). For the SQuAD dataset, Blended RAG achieved an F1 score of 68.4 and an Exact Match (EM) score of 57.63, surpassing fine-tuned models without domain-specific training (p.5).
key_findings: Semantic search-based hybrid queries realize better retrieval precision compared to conventional keyword-based or vector-based searches, with the Sparse Encoder combined with 'Best Fields' often providing superior results (p.5). The Blended RAG framework significantly improves generative Q&A performance even without dataset-specific fine-tuning, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization (p.5, p.6).
limitations: Dense vector indexes require substantially more storage (e.g., 50GB versus 10.5GB for sparse vector indexes on HotPotQA) and have slower querying performance (p.6). Furthermore, datasets devoid of metadata, such as CoQA, do not benefit as impressively from complex hybrid queries because the absence of metadata results in hybrid queries offering no improvement over basic queries (p.6).
title: Blended RAG: Improving RAG (Retriever-Augmented Generation) Accuracy with Semantic Search and Hybrid Query-Based Retrievers
